svg.title: Examples next to the rules. The rule file holds each rule with its expect lines: an address, what should happen, and why. The test command decides every example without counting anything and reports pass or fail, for CI and before a deploy. The rules page and the demo pages show the same examples with the live result and a link to try them, generated from the rule file. A language model can propose expect lines from the rule file and the site's real addresses; a person reviews them before they are kept. Later, a crawl of the site checks that none of its own links is refused.
svg.text: The rule file: each rule with its examples

g.text: expect GET /shop/package passes # a near miss

svg.text: request-shield test site.rules
each example on a fresh store, nothing counted
exit 1 when one fails: before a deploy, in CI
The rules page and the demos
each rule with its examples: the address
(a link to try), what should happen, what
happens now, why -- generated from the file,
so the overview never drifts from the rules
Written by a person -- or proposed by a language model
docs/llm/write-rule-examples.md, given with the rule file:
· per rule: what it refuses, and at least one near miss it must let through
· the site's real addresses (sitemap, a crawl, the log), a comment saying why
· no personal data: documentation address ranges, no cookies, no secrets
then a person reviews them: fixed tests, no model at run time
Later: request-shield crawl site.rules https://www.example.org/
reads the site's pages politely, collects every link and form target,
decides each with the rules: none of the site's own addresses may be refused
(the Exponential rules: 163 links of a real installation, all passing)
Why not generated from the patterns?
a test made from a rule only proves the rule
matches itself; the near misses that matter
are known to the site, not to the pattern
Cost per request: none. expect lines never enter the compiled settings a request loads;
only test, check and the rules page read them.
